slides.lead: Go blank for two minutes. Your baby will notice in seconds.
slides.sub: The still-face experiment, repeated in more than 80 studies since 1978.

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
A parent plays face to face with the baby. Then, on cue, holds a neutral, silent, unresponsive face for a short stretch. Then plays again.

Three brief episodes, back to back. First run in 1978 by Edward Tronick's lab.

slides.head: What babies do when the face goes still

stat.label: reliable changes, across more than 80 studies: less looking at the parent, less smiling, more distress

slides.body: And they work at it. Smiling, reaching, calling out, trying to pull the parent back in before they give up.

slides.head: The catch
slides.body:
A two-minute still face in a lab is not everyday life, and no single blank moment harms a baby. Phones, tiredness and a hard day all produce short stills, and babies recover when you come back.

The effect shows up from about one month, not in newborns.

slides.head: Why it is hopeful
slides.body:
The finding is not that babies need a perfect face. It is that they are built to seek the connection back, and to recover when it returns.

In one small early study, the six-month-olds who kept trying to re-engage were the ones most likely to be securely attached a year later.
